EV_evidence_register.quote: Bio1 (Mean Annual Temperature): This variable is widely recognized as a strong predictor in species distribution models [33]. It provides crucial information about the overall thermal conditions experienced by tree species throughout the year. Areas con limitaciones de pendiente y profundidad, aptas para el
establecimiento de sistemas de cultivos permanentes asociados
con árboles (aislados, en bloques o plantaciones, ya sean espe-
cies frutales y otras con fines de producción de madera y otros
productos forestales). (English: AGROFORESTRY WITH PERMANENT CROPS (Ap): Areas with limitations of slope and depth, suitable for the establishment of permanent crop systems associated with trees (isolated, in blocks or plantations, whether fruit species and others for purposes of timber and other forest product production).)

EV_evidence_register.quote:
The best CEM techniques were diﬀerent for both sites. In Mbeere
South, tied ridging was the best followed by mulching practice while in
Meru South mulching was the best. The tied ridges in the semi-arid site
were hardly destroyed during the cropping season leading to increased
water content in the soil proﬁle and good crop performance while in the
sub-humid site the ridges were repaired often. On clay soils (in Meru
South), ridge tillage can induce water logging, and later on followed by
mass movement/soil erosion (FAO, 1993). Mulching retained more soil
water content in Meru South since the region received more rainfall
compared with Mbeere South. In addition, soils in Meru South are ﬁne
textured, clay while Mbeere South the soils are coarser. Reduced soil
water retention is observed in coarse textured (Mbeere South) than in
ﬁne-textured soils

Often on the sides and the lower end of the cropped area soil bunds are constructed to impede runoff from the cropped area. Cultivated strips are used on flat land or on gentle slopes of up to 4% with at least 1 m deep soils and that receive rainfall of more than 200 mm/y.

relationship.direction: cultivated strips need more than the stated rainfall

EV_evidence_register.quote: Contour forward sloping bench terraces are constructed or develop over time from vegetative strips, contour earth bunds and stone bunds on steeper slopes (up to 60%). relationship.outcome_raw: fuel loads and potential wildfire risk

legacy.qualifier: silvopasture reduces grass biomass, litter, and duff depth, thereby reducing fuel loads and wildfire risk; measured at two Washington State ponderosa pine sites

context.note: migrated v1.5.0→v1.6.0 2026-09-30 (deterministic re-shape, method §10); risk_role=livelihood_mitigation; mitigation_potential=moderate; aez temperate_europe removed 2026-10-02 (US study; T7 has no North-American AEZ id)

EV_evidence_register.quote: This study compared forest composition and structure, fuel types, and vegetative biomass between silvopasture and non-grazed managed forests in Washington, U.S. We show that silvopasture management results in reductions in grass biomass, litter, and duff depth when compared to non-grazed managed forest. These findings point to the integrated nature of silvopasture, where management of overstory composition and structure, understory vegetation, and grazing can reduce fuel loads and potential wildfire risk.
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: fuel loads and potential wildfire risk
EV_evidence_register.attribution: Temperate-US scope (Washington State dryland ponderosa pine forest); Mediterranean studies referenced but not the primary site. Findings may not transfer directly to tropical/subtropical or humid-temperate silvopastoral systems.

context.note: Sign convention: the authors changed the sign of RR for erosion control so beneficial effects are positive (p6). Direction recorded on the outcome as named: soil loss went DOWN. Authors warn the very large effect sizes may reflect publication bias (Kendall tau -0.107, P<0.001). 49 observations for soil loss from 7 studies. | process: strength_class unspecified→strong re-derived from BANDS 2026-10-04 (ratio/ordinal bands added; magnitude unchanged)

EV_evidence_register.quote: Out of seven studies conducted on erosion control, 49 observa- tions were identified for runoff and 49 for soil loss. The studies were conducted in Kenya, Nigeria, and Zimbabwe. Our findings show that agroforestry performed best in terms of erosion reduc- tion ecosystem services, five and ten times better than controls for runoff (RR: 5.0; 95% CI: 3.3-7.9) and soil loss (RR: 9.7; 95% CI: 5.9-17.3). However, these very large effect sizes could also be due to publication bias as demonstrated by the high Kendall’s rank correlation coefficients. If we had found more published studies (larger sample sizes), we expect the effect sizes to be more modest than the figures we reported here. Erosion control with agroforestry was more effective in both humid (RR 7.2; 95% CI 4.8 to 13.9) and semi-arid zones (RR 8.0; 95% CI 4.8 to 16.7) compared to controls. Similarly, erosion control with agroforestry was more effective when either shrubs (RR 6.9; 95% CI 4.6 to 11.4) or trees (RR 11.1; 95% CI 6.1 to 24.7) were planted.

EV_evidence_register.quote: This review shows that agroforestry systems in East Africa stock an average of 24.2 ± 2.8 Mg C ha−1 in biomass and 98.8 ± 12.2 Mg C ha−1 in the soil (Fig. 3). The combined estimate of carbon in biomass and the soil is larger than what was estimated to be the potential carbon storage (29–53 Mg C ha−1) of agrosilvicultural systems in the humid tropics of Africa (Albrecht and Kandji, 2003), but lower than systems with high stem density, large mean tree size, and longer maximum ages i.e. over 60 years reported in Southeast Asia (Roshetko et al., 2007). The difference with earlier estimates is mostly in the soil part where several method­ ological issues need to be considered (Hairiah et al., 2020), such as variation in the soil depth included and changes in soil bulk density that influence which soil is included in a fixed-depth sample (Schrumpf et al., 2011). The amount varies depending on agroforestry practice, ranging from 26.7 ± 7.0 Mg C ha−1 in improved fallows to 153±23 Mg C ha−1 in homegardens.

relationship.outcome_raw: IEG lesson: market-oriented agroforestry (Acacia decurrens) induced transformational change - restoring degraded landscapes, creating employment, generating income and reducing poverty and out-migration - in the microwatersheds where it was supported

EV_evidence_register.quote:
3.6 
Market-oriented agroforestry interventions (for example, Acacia decurrens) that 
bring sustainable income for smallholders can be vital ingredients in creating incentives 
for the adoption of biological measures for land restoration and improving resilience to 
climate shocks. Agroforestry systems, such as Acacia decurrens, that bring additional 
benefits through nitrogen fixation while also generating cash income are vital win-win 
options for land restoration, income growth, and asset creation. The lesson is that in the 
microwatersheds where such market-oriented agroforestry practices have been 
supported (for example, Akusty in Fagita Lekoma, Amhara), this has induced 
transformational changes in restoring highly degraded landscapes, creating 
employment, generating income, and reducing poverty and out-migration.

relationship.outcome_raw: BUNDLED SLM result: 14 of 22 cases rated substantial/high for reducing vulnerability to drought; within that, income growth through commercial agroforestry is named as one option that reduced vulnerability in some communities. The rated effect belongs to the whole SLM package (terracing, bunds, area closure, small-scale irrigation, agroforestry), NOT to agroforestry alone, so no magnitude is encoded.

EV_evidence_register.quote:
Of the 22 cases assessed in the three regions, the responses from the stakeholders 
indicated that 14 cases (63.6 percent) had a substantial or high effect on vulnerability to 
climate shocks (drought). The food security–related effects were highest (i) in areas 
where degradation levels were severe but improvements in land productivity and 
household income have reduced the risk of out-migration, and (ii) in drought-prone 
areas where small-scale irrigation has significantly increased yields and reduced 
vulnerabilities to drought. Also, income growth through commercial agroforestry or 
sustainable charcoal production offered an option for reducing vulnerabilities in some 
communities.

relationship.outcome_raw: milk productivity loss during periods of climate variability 2009-2019: farms with well-established SPS lost 0.4-5.5 percent vs up to 19 percent on extensive conventional cattle-ranching operations
relationship.note: ONTOLOGY/XW GAP: climate_shock has no XW crosswalk row, so this (the lane’s strongest hazard-conditional productivity result) currently routes to no target table. Hazard not disaggregated in the passage ("climate variability" = El Nino/La Nina), so context.hazard_type deliberately left blank.

context.note: World Bank-commissioned climate-variability case study for silvo-pastoral systems, Dec 2019

EV_evidence_register.quote:
72. Contribution to climate resilience. Results of a World Bank study suggest that well-established SPS could help 
reduce vulnerability to climate shocks.47 While extensive CR operations in Colombia reported milk productivity losses 
of up to 19 percent during periods of climate variability from 2009 to 2019, farms with well-established SPS reported 
productivity losses of just 0.4-5.5 percent. Under a scenario where SPS are implemented at scale, projections suggest 
producers could avoid annual losses from climate variability equivalent to 680-2,268M liters of milk and 60,000 tons 
of beef. Unlike traditional, extensive systems, well-established SPS are better adapted to climate shocks because their 
improved vegetative cover and efficient land management reduce vulnerability.
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: milk productivity loss during periods of climate variability

established SPS were more resilient to drought than traditional pastures, these results indicate that SPS are vulnerable to climate 
change in their initial years.

41. Emission reductions via carbon capture were estimated at 1,131,056 t CO2e. As discussed in Section IV A, the 
project made critical contributions to carbon monitoring in Colombian livestock systems. Based on measurements of 
soil carbon content and above-ground biomass, the project developed Tier 3 factors for carbon sequestration for 
each land-use type to measure carbon capture associated with actual farm-level changes in land use.29 Dispersed 
trees in pasturelands, live fences, and iSPS, along with secondary forest conservation, contributed to carbon 
sequestration in all project regions, but particularly the Cesar River Valley. Net accumulated CO2 removals resulting 
from the conversion of pasturelands were estimated at 1,131,056 t CO2e.

(English: In the specific case of silvopastoral systems, establishment and maintenance strategies would require more skilled labour (e.g. for planting seedlings, pruning the trees, etc.), more elaborate infrastructure (e.g. for seedling production) and, above all, a greater number of management decisions, when compared with more traditional and less intensive land-use systems such as pure grass pastures.)

relationship.outcome_raw: cultural barrier: unfounded belief that shading livestock reduces meat or milk output by cutting grazing time

EV_evidence_register.quote: Ademais, em função do desconhecimento e da falta de informações confiáveis, certas dúvidas e mitos ainda persistem no meio rural com relação aos SSPs, levando a certa aversão ao uso desses sistemas. Por exemplo, existe a crença, cientificamente infundada, por parte de alguns produtores, de que o provimento de sombra aos animais na pastagem poderia diminuir a produção de carne ou leite. A justificativa para isso seria que o acesso voluntário à sombra reduziria o tempo de pastejo (i.e., aumentaria o tempo dedicado ao ócio) e, conseqüentemente, o consumo de forragem. (English: Moreover, because of a lack of knowledge and of reliable information, certain doubts and myths still persist in rural areas regarding silvopastoral systems, leading to a certain aversion to using these systems. For example, there is a scientifically unfounded belief among some producers that providing shade to animals in the pasture could reduce meat or milk production. The justification for this would be that voluntary access to shade would reduce grazing time (i.e. increase idle time) and consequently forage intake.)

relationship.outcome_raw: in West Africa planting a tree signifies land tenure, so tenants are legally not allowed to plant trees or establish live fences

context.note: tenure barrier specific to linear/boundary practices

EV_evidence_register.quote: En África Occidental se generan conflictos de intereses por la implantación de cercas vivas, dado que plantar un árbol tiene significado de tenencia de tierra y alinderación de propiedad. Este conflicto afecta directamente la plantación de cercas vivas ya que, por cuestión legal no se permite a los arrendatarios plantar árboles ni mucho menos establecer cercas vivas, ya que esto podría traer problemas legales al momento de heredar. Por lo tanto, en la mayoría de los casos las cercas vivas no surgirían y tendrían que implementar métodos alternos como el caso de cercas muertas (Levasseur et al., 2004). (English: In West Africa conflicts of interest are generated by the establishment of live fences, since planting a tree has the meaning of land tenure and property demarcation. This conflict directly affects the planting of live fences since, for legal reasons, tenants are not allowed to plant trees, let alone establish live fences, as this could bring legal problems at the time of inheritance. Therefore, in most cases live fences would not arise and they would have to implement alternative methods such as dead fences (Levasseur et al., 2004).)
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: conflictos de tenencia por plantar árboles

relationship.outcome_raw: plot-level runoff, infiltration trenches vs no trenches (meta-analysis)

context.region: global review (57 studies, 12 countries, mountain regions)
context.note: Plot-scale meta-analysis by the review authors. The source files this result under its 'Reducción de la escorrentía e inundaciones' (peak-flow / flood) ecosystem service (Table 1, p.6); hazard_type=flood per that framing, but all pooled studies were plot-level. Infiltration trenches assigned to water_harvesting__in_situ (contour structures holding rain on the slope where it falls; no separate cropped receiving basin).

EV_evidence_register.quote: Entre los once estudios que midieron la escorrentía en 52 parcelas, todos mostraron una reducción en la escorrentía como resultado de las zanjas de infiltración. El análisis estadístico mostró que las zanjas de infiltración reducen significativamente la escorrentía. En promedio en los estudios anali- zados, las zanjas de infiltración redujeron la escorrentía en un 46.4%. En valores relativos esta reducción representa el 5.7% de la lluvia en promedio. (English: Among the eleven studies that measured runoff on 52 plots, all showed a reduction in runoff as a result of infiltration trenches. The statistical analysis showed that infiltration trenches significantly reduce runoff. On average in the studies analysed, infiltration trenches reduced runoff by 46.4%. In relative values this reduction represents 5.7% of rainfall on average.)

EV_evidence_register.quote: Entre los once estudios que midieron la pérdida de suelo en cincuenta parcelas, todos menos uno reportaron una reducción en la pérdida de suelo como resultado de las zanjas de infiltración. El análisis estadístico mostró que las zanjas de infiltración redujeron significativa y considerablemente la pérdida de suelo. En promedio, las zanjas de infiltración redujeron la pérdida de suelo en un 73.0%. En valores absolutos, esto representa una reducción de 4.8 toneladas por hectárea por año en promedio. (English: Among the eleven studies that measured soil loss on fifty plots, all but one reported a reduction in soil loss as a result of infiltration trenches. Por ejemplo, un estudio identificó un aumento en la concentración de sedimentos en una cuenca durante los primeros dos años después de que se establecieron las zanjas, antes de que la pérdida de suelo se redujera durante tres años y finalmente regresara a una tasa normal20, lo que cuestiona el balance de las zanjas. (English: Some studies found negative impacts right after trench establishment. For example, one study identified an increase in sediment concentration in a catchment during the first two years after the trenches were established, before soil loss fell for three years and finally returned to a normal rate, which calls the balance of trenches into question.)

EV_evidence_register.quote: Ocorre que, no entanto, mesmo com as cisternas, o carro-pipa continuou sendo uma realidade neces­ sária no semiárido e as pessoas continuam sujeitas à tentativa de uso político, porque a falta de água as coloca em uma situação muito vulnerável, como no caso das grandes secas plurianuais, explica a coordenadora local do MOC na Bahia: Então, imagina quando seca tudo. E a água da cis­ terna vai acabando. Como é que não dou um pote de água para meus bodes, minhas galinhas? Aí, o vereador chega lá e diz “não se preocupe, eu vou te dar um pipa”. Se, nesse momento, aquele vereador manda uma água para aquela família, ela vai ficar com um sentimento de gratidão [...]. Então, mas a água é um direito, e o direito não pode ser negociado. (Entrevista 5; Arsky 2019). (English: It happens, however, that even with the cisterns, the water truck continued to be a necessary reality in the semi-arid and people remain subject to attempts at political use, because the lack of water puts them in a very vulnerable situation, as in the case of the great multi-year droughts, explains the local MOC coordinator in Bahia: So, imagine when everything dries up. And the cistern water runs out. How can I not give a pot of water to my goats, my chickens? Then the councillor arrives and says 'don't worry, I'll give you a truckload'. If at that moment that councillor sends water to that family, she will feel gratitude [...]. But water is a right, and a right cannot be negotiated. (Interview 5; Arsky 2019).)

Resultado de um consistente processo de capacitação e conscien­ tização, existe hoje uma verdadeira cultura sobre o gerenciamento da água armazenada na cisterna, e a água de beber armazenada é tratada com zelo e cuidado. Essa reserva adicional, essa poupança, adia ou até mesmo evita as situações limites em que viviam essas famílias. (English: In addition, it conferred autonomy, because the benefiting family 'manages to go without depending on the water truck. It was very easy to perceive, in direct field observation, how the categories of dignity and autonomy present themselves. As a result of a consistent process of training and awareness-raising, there is today a true culture of managing the water stored in the cistern, and the stored drinking water is treated with zeal and care. This additional reserve, this saving, postpones or even avoids the extreme situations in which these families used to live.)

[...] Foi bom depois dessa água. Até agora mesmo, os tanques de barro estão secos e os animais estão se abastecendo da cisterna. A gente até parou de plantar um pouco, porque estamos poupando para os animais. [...] Se não fosse ela [a água estocada na cisterna] não dava. Porque a água da EMBASA [Empresa Baiana de Águas e Saneamento] não dá, porque passa da taxa. E, também, nós nem teríamos como armazenar, porque a água vem de oito em oito dias, e nós aqui em cima somos o último a receber, então quando chega nossa vez, já é hora de acabar de novo [...]. A água que tá na cisterna é da chuva e ainda tem como segurar alguns meses. (English: We had difficulty with water, because from where we live to the fields, to the tanks, it is quite far, and now not, because we got the cistern with a pump, and the extension comes with the project itself. [...] It was good after this water. Even right now, the clay tanks are dry and the animals are drinking from the cistern. We even stopped planting a bit, because we are saving it for the animals. [...] If it weren't for it [the water stored in the cistern] it wouldn't be possible. Because the EMBASA [Bahia water and sanitation company] water isn't enough, because it exceeds the fee. relationship.outcome_raw: cisterns (consumption + production) credited with a large reduction in rural establishments without any water source (census-based inference, no counterfactual)

context.note: IPEA review author's inference from Censo Agropecuario 2017 counts; mixes consumption (rooftop) and production cisterns, modal = rooftop consumption cisterns

EV_evidence_register.quote: De todo modo, das mais de 1 milhão de cisternas de consumo e produção construídas, a maio­ ria encontra-se no meio rural (tabela 4) e, nesse sentido, é inegável sua significativa contribuição para a ampliação do acesso à água na região. Considerando-se que em 2017 aproximadamente 446 mil estabelecimentos agropecuários no semiárido não possuíam acesso à nenhuma fonte hídrica,16 havendo um número de mais de 1 milhão de cisternas construídas, boa parte das quais no semiárido e no meio rural, é fácil concluir que o número de estabelecimentos, principalmente familiares (tabela 4), e, consequentemente, pessoas sem acesso à água seria muito maior. Esses dados confirmam que, justamente onde esperado, no meio rural, as cisternas contribuem de modo evidente, com a consecução da meta 6.1 do ODS da água. (English: In any case, of the more than 1 million consumption and production cisterns built, most are in rural areas (table 4) and, in this sense, their significant contribution to expanding access to water in the region is undeniable. Considering that in 2017 approximately 446 thousand agricultural establishments in the semi-arid had no access to any water source,16 with more than 1 million cisterns built, a good part of them in the semi-arid and in rural areas, it is easy to conclude that the number of establishments, mainly family farms (table 4), and consequently of people without access to water would be much greater. These data confirm that, exactly where expected, in rural areas, cisterns contribute clearly to achieving SDG target 6.1 on water.)

EV_evidence_register.quote: A barragem subterrânea de maior porte, como as construídas na região de Mutuca, pode proporcionar projetos de pequena irrigação e gerar renda direta e indireta para os proprietários da terra e a comunidade. Foram claros os melhoramentos da produção agrícola, com proprietários colhendo até 4 safras contínuas em 12 meses. É importante aqui ressaltar a tradição e ex- periência no local para esse tipo de atividade, o que não ocorre, por exemplo, em São Caetano. (English: The larger subsurface dam, such as those built in the Mutuca region, can provide small irrigation projects and generate direct and indirect income for landowners and the community. Improvements in agricultural production were clear, with owners harvesting up to 4 continuous crops in 12 months. It is important to stress here the local tradition and experience in this type of activity, which does not occur, for example, in Sao Caetano.)

relationship.outcome_raw: runoff-harvesting pond (barreiro) water applied as supplemental irrigation during in-season dry spells reduces crop-loss risk

context.note: hazard = in-season dry spells (veranicos), i.e. agricultural drought; institutional statement, no data in passage; barreiro = small earth reservoir fed by a micro-catchment; COI: Embrapa Semiarido self-assessment of technologies it developed/promotes

EV_evidence_register.quote: tre estas tecnologias, o uso da irrigação de salvação tem reduzido os riscos da exploração agrícola em anos cuja precipitação pluviométrica é irregular, proporcionando até duas colheitas em anos considerados normais de chuvas. Segundo Porto et al. (1983), no Semi-Árido brasi- leiro, três em cada dez anos são considerados normais com relação à quantidade e à distribuição das chuvas. Define-se a irrigação de salvação como a lâmina de água aplicada à cul- tura nos veranicos que comumente ocorrem durante o período chuvoso na região Nordeste, de forma a não permitir que a cultura sofra estresse hídrico e, em alguns casos, morra. No Semi-Árido brasileiro, após as pri- meiras chuvas, é comum ocorrerem períodos de 20 a 30 dias sem novas chuvas, comprometendo seriamente a germinação e outras fases de de- senvolvimento das culturas. (English: [Am]ong these technologies, supplemental (salvation) irrigation has reduced the risks of farming in years with irregular rainfall, allowing up to two harvests in years considered normal. According to Porto et al. (1983), in the Brazilian semi-arid three in every ten years are considered normal in rainfall quantity and distribution. Salvation irrigation is defined as the depth of water applied to the crop during the dry spells (veranicos) that commonly occur during the rainy season in the Northeast, so as not to let the crop suffer water stress and, in some cases, die. In the Brazilian semi-arid, after the first rains, periods of 20 to 30 days without new rain are common, seriously compromising germination and other crop development phases.)

Otro estudio en México mostró que 16 de 24 zanjas se llenaron al 50% de su volumen después de menos de cuatro años y que todas las zanjas establecidas se llenarían por completo después de once años19. (English: Studies that analysed how infiltration trenches evolve over time show short-term impacts: as infiltration trenches gradually fill with sediment, their performance declines. For example, in a study in Ethiopia, trenches were effective at reducing runoff and erosion for only two or three years. Another study in Mexico showed that 16 of 24 trenches filled to 50% of their volume after less than four years and that all established trenches would fill completely after eleven years.)

relationship.outcome_raw: construction and siting failures of subsurface dams traced to lack of technical follow-up

EV_evidence_register.quote: Problemas construtivos - Os principais problemas cons- trutivos detectados em algumas das barragens subterrâneas foram: • Erro de locação: local impróprio por apresentar bacia de contribuição pequena, e assim baixa capacidade de retenção de água; • Escavação insuficiente, sem alcançar a rocha no fundo da aluvião; • Problema com a lona na hora de sua colocação, sem alcançar o leito rochoso, permitindo fuga por baixo; • Solos com baixo nível de infiltração; • Poço com baixa permeabilidade, dificultando a entra- da de água; • Barragens construídas em solos salinizáveis. Esses problemas ocorreram em diferentes locais, em decorrência quase sempre da falta de acompanhamento técnico adequado. (English: Construction problems - The main construction problems detected in some of the subsurface dams were: siting error (improper site with a small contributing basin and so low water-retention capacity); insufficient excavation not reaching bedrock; problems with the plastic sheet during placement, not reaching bedrock and allowing leakage underneath; soils with low infiltration; well with low permeability hindering water entry; dams built in salinisable soils. These problems occurred in different places, almost always as a result of lack of adequate technical follow-up.)
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: construction and siting failures of subsurface dams traced to lack of technical follow-up

relationship.outcome_raw: seedling mortality from short-term (minutes) exposure to extreme heat

context.note: perspective; terrestrial plant restoration by seeding/outplanting, not forest-specific

EV_evidence_register.quote: Even short-­term exposure to extreme heat (minutes) can cause seedling mortality in many species (Teskey et al., 2015).

relationship.outcome_raw: complete restoration failure attributed to novel drought, even with outplantings

context.note: perspective; terrestrial plant restoration incl. outplantings, not forest-specific

EV_evidence_register.quote: Novel levels of drought alone are attributed with causing complete ecological restoration failure, even when inten- sive restoration methods such as outplantings that have historically demonstrated successful establishment are utilized (Rader et al., 2022).

relationship.outcome_raw: high seedling mortality from record drought followed by flooding year

context.note: perspective; drought-then-flood sequence; also drought-relevant; not forest-specific

EV_evidence_register.quote: Consecutive years of extreme climatic conditions, such as a year with a record drought followed by a year of heavy precipitation and flooding, both of which can lead to high seedling mortality, may also occur (Doherty & Zedler, 2015).

relationship.outcome_raw: increasing mortality of recently outplanted seedlings in dry regions attributed to hotter/drier conditions

context.region: western North America (and arid regions worldwide)
context.note: review; highest mortality in first few years after outplanting (same paragraph)

EV_evidence_register.lineage_of: Raftoyannis 2006; Vallejo 2012; del Campo 2021 et al.
EV_evidence_register.quote: Increasing mortality of recently outplanted seedlings in dry regions is being attributed to hotter and/or drier conditions intensifying the planting-stress phenomenon (Raftoyannis et al. 2006; Vallejo et al. 2012; Ouzts et al. 2015; Pardos et al. 2015; Sukhbaatar et al. 2020; del Campo et al. 2021).

relationship.outcome_raw: heat stress in outplanted seedlings on open restoration sites (seedling-height air 10 °C above 2 m air)

context.region: western North America (and arid regions worldwide)
context.note: microclimate after overstory removal by harvest or fire

EV_evidence_register.quote: During the growing season, open forest restoration sites have microsites where outplanted seedlings are exposed to air temperature at seedling height, which is 10 °C higher than air temperature at 2 m (with soil or litter surfaces being up to 30 °C higher) (Geiger 1980; Spittlehouse and Stathers 1990). Such temperatures cause heat stress in seedlings.

relationship.outcome_raw: high seedling mortality on restoration sites under low soil water, high temperature and VPD

context.region: western North America (and arid regions worldwide)
context.note: conditions = lower soil water + higher temperature + higher VPD

EV_evidence_register.quote: Such limiting conditions in the energy and hydrologic cycles at restoration sites in western North America (Davis et al. 2019) have resulted in high rates of seedling mortality (Petrie et al. 2016, 2023; Hankin et al. 2019; Chen and Nelson 2020; Hill and Ex 2020; Rodman et al. 2020; Crockett and Hurteau 2022; Marsh et al. 2022; Davis et al. 2023).

relationship.outcome_raw: 3-month SPI drought index vs temporal evolution of plantation mortality (r = -0.72; negative SPI = drought)

context.note: 709 ha reforestation project, 7 native species, 10-yr monitoring

EV_evidence_register.quote: Finally, the drought index (SPI), which only has tempo- ral variation (same value for all plots on the same date), correlated strongly with the temporal evolution of mortality (r = −0.72; p < 0.01).

relationship.outcome_raw: mid-to-high mortality in establishment; worsened in mid-term due to exceptional severe drought

context.note: total mortality 83% after ten years (stated p11); driest year on record

EV_evidence_register.quote: In the short term (establishment phase), when meteorological constraints were almost absent (only a short, acute drought between April and August 2009), mortality can be considered as mid-to-high, with about one quarter of the plantation dead by the ﬁrst year, and more than half in the second year. In the mid-term, this trend worsened due to an exceptional, severe drought.

relationship.outcome_raw: extreme drought reveals years later the impact of inappropriate technical measures on plantation mortality

context.note: interaction drought x technical decisions (tree shelters)

EV_evidence_register.quote: Therefore, although the technical factors showed greater impact in the short- than in the mid-term, our results suggest that environmental events such as the extreme drought recorded here can reveal, several years later, the impact of inappropriate technical measures that would otherwise remain concealed.

relationship.outcome_raw: tree shelters blown away by windstorms (and poor tethering) by end of 2008

context.note: damage to planting protection equipment, partly attributed to poor tethering

EV_evidence_register.quote: Also, seedlings that had their tree shelters blown away by the end of 2008, due to wind- storms and poor tethering, were included in this regard (Table 2).

relationship.outcome_raw: above-ground carbon sequestration potential of natural regeneration over 215 Mha in 30 years

EV_evidence_register.quote: On the basis of recent spatially explicit assessments of above-ground carbon accumulation potential from natural regeneration10, we esti- mate that forest regeneration over this 215 Mha could sequester 23.4 Gt of C (range, 21.1–25.7) in aboveground biomass alone over a 30 year period if these potential regrowing forests have the oppor- tunity to establish and persist

relationship.outcome_raw: tree-planting-based reforestation can reduce biodiversity benefits where forests could regenerate naturally

EV_evidence_register.quote: However, in contexts in which forests can regenerate naturally or with some assistance, reforestation based on tree planting can actually reduce biodiversity conservation benefits if selected tree species or management practices do not provide suitable habitat for species of conservation concern or for keystone species39.

relationship.outcome_raw: young regenerating forests fail to persist, incl. due to vulnerability to fire

context.note: also market shifts, perverse policies (see operational units)

EV_evidence_register.quote: Young forests fail to persist for many rea- sons, including market shifts, perverse policies, vulnerability to fire and a lack of awareness of the benefits they provide42.

relationship.outcome_raw: natural regeneration cost per ha vs forest restoration projects (US$105-25,830)

context.note: cited range; price year not stated

EV_evidence_register.quote: In areas where ecological conditions are such that forests can grow back on their own or with low-cost assistance, natural regeneration methods are less costly (for example, US$12–3,880 per ha compared with US$105–25,830 for forest restoration projects in the tropics and subtropics15) and often are more effective than full tree planting in terms of their long-term success rates and biodiversity outcomes3.

relationship.outcome_raw: cost per ha of forest restoration projects in the tropics and subtropics (pooled; comparator to natural regeneration US$12-3,880)

context.note: pooled restoration projects, no isolated family; cited range; price year not stated

EV_evidence_register.quote: In areas where ecological conditions are such that forests can grow back on their own or with low-cost assistance, natural regeneration methods are less costly (for example, US$12–3,880 per ha compared with US$105–25,830 for forest restoration projects in the tropics and subtropics15) and often are more effective than full tree planting in terms of their long-term success rates and biodiversity outcomes3.

relationship.outcome_raw: tree species richness vs time since disturbance (secondary succession chronosequence, 18 forests)

EV_evidence_register.quote: The species richness was a function (r2 = 0.54, F1;17 = 18.19, P = 0.0007) of the time after disturbance (Fig. 3a).

relationship.outcome_raw: time for secondary forest to reach 80% animal-dispersed species

EV_evidence_register.quote: From the model it was possible to estimate that a forest needs 65 years (range: 23–178 years) to achieve a proportion of 80% of animal-dis- persed species.

relationship.outcome_raw: time for secondary forest to recover mature-forest endemism (40%): ~2000 years

context.note: very slow recovery of endemism; positive but negligible within project horizons

EV_evidence_register.quote: From the regression it was possible to estimate that 1987 years (range: 860–4592) are necessary after a disturbance to reach the percentage of endemism that occur in mature forests (40%).

relationship.outcome_raw: total above-ground biomass of 25-y first-cycle secondary regrowth (50% of mature forest)

context.note: fallow regrowth after slash-and-burn; biomass not carbon

EV_evidence_register.quote: Secondary forests accumulated 50% (i.e. 229 t ha−1) of mature forest biomass after 25 y of ﬁrst-cycle regrowth.

relationship.outcome_raw: water yield (P-ET) change 2041-2070 under full reforestation potential, Loess Plateau-North China Plain

context.note: regional coupled land-climate model, RCP4.5; reforestation scenario

EV_evidence_register.quote: An increase in water yield was shown in 7 of 15 regions, which was statistically significant in four regions—­Loess Plateau–­North China Plain (11.4 ± 11.8%), Yangtze Plain (16.9 ± 3.3%), Southeast China (17.6 ± 6.4%), and Irrawaddy (84.9 ± 24.7%) (Table 1).

relationship.outcome_raw: water yield (P-ET) change 2041-2070 under full reforestation potential, Yangtze Plain

context.note: regional coupled land-climate model, RCP4.5; reforestation scenario

EV_evidence_register.quote: An increase in water yield was shown in 7 of 15 regions, which was statistically significant in four regions—­Loess Plateau–­North China Plain (11.4 ± 11.8%), Yangtze Plain (16.9 ± 3.3%), Southeast China (17.6 ± 6.4%), and Irrawaddy (84.9 ± 24.7%) (Table 1).

relationship.outcome_raw: water yield (P-ET) change 2041-2070 under full reforestation potential, Southeast China

context.note: regional coupled land-climate model, RCP4.5; reforestation scenario

EV_evidence_register.quote: An increase in water yield was shown in 7 of 15 regions, which was statistically significant in four regions—­Loess Plateau–­North China Plain (11.4 ± 11.8%), Yangtze Plain (16.9 ± 3.3%), Southeast China (17.6 ± 6.4%), and Irrawaddy (84.9 ± 24.7%) (Table 1).

relationship.outcome_raw: water yield (P-ET) change 2041-2070 under full reforestation potential, Irrawaddy

context.note: regional coupled land-climate model, RCP4.5; reforestation scenario

EV_evidence_register.quote: An increase in water yield was shown in 7 of 15 regions, which was statistically significant in four regions—­Loess Plateau–­North China Plain (11.4 ± 11.8%), Yangtze Plain (16.9 ± 3.3%), Southeast China (17.6 ± 6.4%), and Irrawaddy (84.9 ± 24.7%) (Table 1).

relationship.outcome_raw: nonsignificant declines in net water yield in some regions from heightened ET

context.note: declines e.g. Murray-Darling, Manchurian Plain (Table 1); none significant

EV_evidence_register.quote: However, some regions experience nonsignificant declines in net water yield due to heightened evapotranspiration outstripping increases in precipitation, or de- clines in soil moisture and advected precipitation.

relationship.outcome_raw: probability of extremely dry months (lowest monthly P at 50-yr return interval) declined in 9 of 15 regions

context.note: Table 2: most regional changes not significant; Irrawaddy significant in the adverse direction

EV_evidence_register.quote: Reforestation was broadly shown to reduce the probability of extremely dry months (Table 2), especially in regions with an in- crease in total annual precipitation. A decline in extreme dry events (lowest monthly precipitation occurring at a 50-­year return interval) was observed in 9 of 15 regions, of which six regions had an increase in annual total precipitation.

relationship.outcome_raw: simulated July 2001 flood peak discharge, reforestation (+50% forest) vs present land use

context.note: WetSpa model; grassland converted to forest, cover 49.8% to 75.3%

EV_evidence_register.quote: The simulated peak discharge for the present land use is 84.8 m3/s, and for the reforestation scenario this becomes 74.9 m3/s, which means the scenario decreases the peak discharge by 12%.

relationship.outcome_raw: average peak discharge reduction over the simulation period

context.note: WetSpa model; +50% forest

EV_evidence_register.quote: Investigation of peak discharges for the whole simulation period, shows that the reforestation scenario results in a reduction of 18% on average.

relationship.outcome_raw: peak flow reduction for 80 mm storms of 5-20 h duration; larger for short intense storms

context.note: synthetic rain-duration test

EV_evidence_register.quote: The reforestation scenario reduces the peak by 29% for the shortest rain duration and only 17% for the longest one. These results show that for a 50% increase of forest in the basin there is a signiﬁcant reduction of peak ﬂows of about 24% on average, but the effect becomes less if the rain continues for a longer time.

relationship.outcome_raw: reforestation decreases surface runoff and flood volume

EV_evidence_register.quote: Reforestation results in decreasing surface runoff and ﬂood volume, but increasing amounts of interﬂow and baseﬂow, as well as soil moisture and evapotranspiration.

relationship.outcome_raw: peak flow reduction, forestation of all arable land (~66% of basin)

context.note: study basin/country not stated in passage

EV_evidence_register.quote: Lahmer et al. (2001) presented a forestation scenario assuming the conversion of all the arable land (about 66% of the total basin area) to forest that reduced peak ﬂow by 42.3%.

relationship.outcome_raw: flood peak reduction, afforestation scenario +53% forest, Alzette basin

EV_evidence_register.quote: The simulation of Liu and De Smedt (2004) shows the afforestation decreases the peak by 8%.

relationship.outcome_raw: sediment concentration in runoff, sparse/no tree cover plot vs good-cover plot in eucalyptus afforestation

context.note: eucalyptus afforestation (1968) of former rangeland; plots P1 vs P2, 10 events

EV_evidence_register.quote: For all events, the sediment concentrations listed for plot P1 are substantially greater than those from plot 2. This difference further conﬁrms the increased erosion rates associated with areas with little or no tree cover in catchment W2, as represented by plot P1, and therefore the importance of the forest canopy in reducing erosion.

relationship.outcome_raw: germination reduced by lack of rainfall; seedlings scorched by direct sun (Beilschmiedia)

EV_evidence_register.quote: In addition, seed germination was sharply reduced by lack of rainfall and the seedlings were highly susceptible to scorching by direct sunlight.

relationship.outcome_raw: germination in full sunlight reduced by dry-season drought (Prunus cerasoides, nursery experiment)

context.note: nursery experiment simulating dry-season drought

EV_evidence_register.quote: In full sunlight, ger- mination was signiﬁcantly reduced by dry season drought but remained high when seeds were watered.

relationship.outcome_raw: natural recruitment of 36 tree seedling species beneath 8-yr-old framework-species plantings

context.note: framework species method (FORRU-CMU); no unplanted control reported

EV_evidence_register.quote: Thirty-six tree seedling species were found beneath the selected trees, of which 11 were wind-dispersed and 25 were animal-dispersed.

relationship.outcome_raw: 4-yr mortality of planted seedlings in flood-prone depressions vs dry sandbanks: no significant difference

context.note: depressions prone to seasonal flooding 10-30 days/yr (p3); nucleation rings

EV_evidence_register.quote: There was no statistical difference in total mortality between the depressions (53%) and sandbanks (46.5%) over the four-year interval (t = −1.6638, P = 0.1029).

relationship.outcome_raw: branch breakage and damage to seedlings from strong constant wind

EV_evidence_register.quote: Strong and constant wind in rest- inga vegetation causes branches to break and other damage to seedlings, directly affecting height growth (Zamith & Scarano 2006).

relationship.outcome_raw: natural regeneration of native zoochoric species under artificial perches (none in planted rings)

context.note: 17 of 25 perches had regenerants

EV_evidence_register.quote: The absence of regener- ants in the planted rings suggest that the artiﬁcial perch technique was efﬁcient and important to accel- erate the regeneration of some native zoochoric spe- cies in the restoration areas.

relationship.outcome_raw: artificial perches increase seed and seedling abundance and richness vs control sites without perches

EV_evidence_register.quote: Our results also corroborate Guidetti et al. (2016) who found that setting-up artiﬁcial perches in open areas increases the abundance and richness of seeds and seedlings compared to control sites without perches.

relationship.outcome_raw: natural regeneration has lower cost (vs planting)

relationship.outcome_raw: water yield (streamflow) after forestation

context.note: ONTOLOGY GAP: no VONT id for annual water yield / streamflow; recorded under water_regulation (flow-regulation component) - ontology triage; review: mostly plantation forestry, few humid-tropics studies

EV_evidence_register.quote: In a review of forestation effects on streamflow by Filoso et al. (2017), most studies reported decreases in water yields following the intervention. However, most studies referred to plantation forestry rather than forest restoration with mostly slower growing native species.

relationship.outcome_raw: water transmission fraction Q/P, forest vs non-forest (global watershed dataset)

context.note: ONTOLOGY GAP: no VONT id for annual water yield / streamflow; recorded under water_regulation (flow-regulation component) - ontology triage; land-cover comparison, no intervention isolated; differences may not hold locally (same page)

EV_evidence_register.lineage_of: Zhou et al. 2015; Zhang et al. 2017
EV_evidence_register.quote: The weighted average based on the global distribution of P/Epot ratios (Figure 2.2A) indicates a global mean water transmission fraction for forests and non-forests of 33.8 and 40.8%, respectively
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: water transmission fraction Q/P, forest vs non-forest (global watershed dataset)
EV_evidence_register.attribution: Zhou et al. 2015; Zhang et al. 2017

relationship.outcome_raw: dry-season streamflow of 25-45-yr native-species plantations vs old growth

context.note: ONTOLOGY GAP: no VONT id for annual water yield / streamflow; recorded under water_regulation (flow-regulation component) - ontology triage; 'exceeding 50%' deficit

EV_evidence_register.quote: Because of high water use by young, densely-spaced trees, for- est plantations of native tree species aged 25 to 45 years produce persistent dry-season streamflow deficits ex- ceeding 50% relative to native old-growth forests (Perry and Jones, 2017).
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: dry-season streamflow of 25-45-yr native-species plantations vs old growth

relationship.outcome_raw: flood risk after conversion of natural forest to plantation crops / urban

context.note: adequate controls for confounders; most correlational forest-flood evidence contested (same page)

EV_evidence_register.quote: However, the analysis of Malaysian data by Tan-Soo et al. (2014) with adequate controls of confounding factors showed increased flood risk after conversion from natural forest to plantation crops and urbanization.
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: flood risk after conversion of natural forest to plantation crops / urban

relationship.outcome_raw: snowmelt flood risk in valleys with >30% forest cover

context.note: 1920s Swiss valley comparison; 30% 'safe threshold'; snowmelt floods only

EV_evidence_register.quote: In valleys with more than 30%, forest snowmelt was more gradual and flooding risk was lower, than in valleys where all snow could melt simultaneously.
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: snowmelt flood risk in valleys with >30% forest cover

relationship.outcome_raw: peak flows after forest harvest in small and large (100-1,000 km2) basins

context.note: Pacific Northwest; partial harvest smaller effects (same page)

EV_evidence_register.quote: forest harvest was associated with significant increases in peak flows in both small and large (100 - 1,000 km2) basins (Jones and Grant, 1996; Jones, 2000).
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: peak flows after forest harvest in small and large (100-1,000 km2) basins

relationship.outcome_raw: upland tree cutting NOT the cause of large-basin downstream flooding (THED refuted)

context.note: LARGE-BASIN NULL kept: forest cover does not control large-river floods

EV_evidence_register.quote: Essentially what was proven was that, while the Himalayas were facing severe development and environmental challenges, a growing peasant population cutting trees was not the reason for flooding in the downstream plains.
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: downstream (Ganga/Bangladesh plains) flooding vs Himalayan tree cutting

relationship.outcome_raw: soil erosion and sediment under China's reforestation/afforestation programmes

context.note: national programmes (NFPP, SLCP etc.); also increased carbon, improved flow patterns

EV_evidence_register.quote: The implementation of all those programmes has increased forest cover signif- icantly while having positive environmental consequences (e.g., reduced soil erosion and sediments, increased carbon stocks, improved flow patterns) in China (Ran et al., 2013).
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: soil erosion and sediment under China's reforestation/afforestation programmes

relationship.outcome_raw: splash erosion (soil detachment) under plantations without understory

context.note: adverse effect of understory-free plantations

EV_evidence_register.quote: Forest plantations without understory can increase the kinetic energy of throughfall beyond that of rainfall and increase detach- ment of soil particles as a first stage of erosion (Wiersum, 1991).
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: splash erosion (soil detachment) under plantations without understory

relationship.outcome_raw: erosion under afforestation

context.note: trade-off with water yield (paired unit)

EV_evidence_register.quote: Trade-offs can also involve erosion regula- tion and water yields, whereas afforestation can provide relevant erosion reduction benefits while reducing water yield (Dymond et al., 2012).

relationship.outcome_raw: water yield under afforestation

context.note: ONTOLOGY GAP: no VONT id for annual water yield / streamflow; recorded under water_regulation (flow-regulation component) - ontology triage; trade-off with erosion reduction

EV_evidence_register.quote: Trade-offs can also involve erosion regula- tion and water yields, whereas afforestation can provide relevant erosion reduction benefits while reducing water yield (Dymond et al., 2012).

relationship.outcome_raw: gully erosion and landslides on abandoned terraced land

context.note: land abandonment (spontaneous regrowth) on former terraces - adverse | landslide (event) evidence filed under erosion — 8b B (Pete 2026-10-07): landslide is an asset-threat-only hazard; no livelihood cell

EV_evidence_register.quote: Abandoned land in previously terraced landscapes was found to be particularly prone to gully erosion and landslides (Tarolli et al., 2014), while in other instances, land abandonment and increase in the area of forests and grasslands led to a decrease in soil erosion (Latocha et al., 2016).
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: gully erosion and landslides on abandoned terraced land

relationship.outcome_raw: soil erosion after land abandonment with forest/grassland expansion

context.note: land abandonment -> forest/grassland increase - beneficial | landslide (event) evidence filed under erosion — 8b B (Pete 2026-10-07): landslide is an asset-threat-only hazard; no livelihood cell

EV_evidence_register.quote: Abandoned land in previously terraced landscapes was found to be particularly prone to gully erosion and landslides (Tarolli et al., 2014), while in other instances, land abandonment and increase in the area of forests and grasslands led to a decrease in soil erosion (Latocha et al., 2016).
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: soil erosion after land abandonment with forest/grassland expansion

relationship.outcome_raw: recovery of infiltration and recharge after forest cover increase

context.note: GFEP panel conclusion: belowground (infiltration/recharge) recovery takes decades

EV_evidence_register.quote: Furthermore, the recovery of aboveground benefits is feasible within a few years, but recovery of belowground benefits (i.e., infiltration and recharge) is often a slower process, counted in dec- ades rather than years.
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: recovery of infiltration and recharge after forest cover increase

relationship.outcome_raw: poverty / well-being near protected areas

context.note: XW GAP: rural_poverty as ev_variable has no route (needs rural_poverty -> T6 rural_poverty direct); effect lower for remote PAs (roads moderate, same page)

EV_evidence_register.lineage_of: Andam et al. 2010; den Braber et al. 2018; Naidoo et al. 2018
EV_evidence_register.quote: Several large-scale data-driven studies that specif- ically sought to control for numerous so- cio-economic factors, have demonstrated that protected areas can be key drivers of poverty reduction and improved well-be- ing (Andam et al., 2010; den Braber et al., 2018; Naidoo et al., 2018, Figure 4.2a).
EV_evidence_register.attribution: Andam et al. 2010; den Braber et al. 2018; Naidoo et al. 2018

relationship.outcome_raw: 68% of 697 CFM cases reporting livelihood outcomes showed income increases (vote count, not effect size)

context.note: systematic review, predominantly South Asian, qualitative cases; evidence strength judged lacking (same page)

EV_evidence_register.quote: In their recent authoritative review of availa- ble evidence on community forests examining 697 published cases of CFM, Hajjar et al. (2016) found that 68% of cases that reported on livelihood out- comes indicated that community or household in- comes increased after CFM implementation.

relationship.outcome_raw: households in poverty, villages with vs without CFM, 2000-2012

context.note: XW GAP: rural_poverty as ev_variable has no route (needs rural_poverty -> T6 rural_poverty direct)

EV_evidence_register.quote: In a rigorous analysis of 18,000 community forests in Nepal, Oldekop et al. (2019) show that CFM reduced both poverty and deforest- ation (Box 5.1).
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: households in poverty, villages with vs without CFM, 2000-2012

relationship.outcome_raw: deforestation under CFM (forest cover retained)

context.note: XW GAP: landscape_forest_cover has no route

EV_evidence_register.quote: In a rigorous analysis of 18,000 community forests in Nepal, Oldekop et al. (2019) show that CFM reduced both poverty and deforest- ation (Box 5.1).

relationship.outcome_raw: household living standards (consumption-based) under CFM

context.note: 'small but positive'; living standards recorded under household_income (nearest id)

context.note: technique: nursery (fall) nutrient loading vs uptake from site soil; review of western North America and arid restoration sites worldwide

EV_evidence_register.quote: Nutrient loading in the nursery is a more efficient approach to nutrient acquisition by seedlings compared with nutrient uptake from soil at the outplanting site (Tinus 1974; Binkley 1986), and results in rapid shoot and root growth after outplanting (Grossnickle and MacDonald 2018), thus improving seedling survival (Grossnickle 2012)

EV_evidence_register.quote: Finally, although studies show a benefi­ cial seedling response to fall nutrient loading, there are instances where this practice had no effect on seedling field performance (Grossnickle 2012; Grossnickle and MacDonald 2018). This has been attributed to either sufficient nutrient availability at the outplanting site (Andivia et al. 2011) or other growth-limiting site factors (e.g., low available soil water) (Wang et al. 2015).

relationship.outcome_raw: flood damage during a tropical storm avoided by existing wetlands and floodplains (Otter Creek watershed)

context.note: measured on EXISTING wetlands/floodplains (protection value), cited as illustrating the benefit of restoring floodplain wetlands; no comparator vocab exists for existing wetlands (existing_forest only); clean-up savings reported as a watershed total with no per-unit denominator, not encoded

EV_evidence_register.quote:
During a recent tropical storm, wetlands and floodplains in 
the Otter Creek watershed in Vermont, U.S.A., reduced flood damage by an estimated 84% to 
95%, saving between USD 126,000 and 450,000 in clean-up costs (Watson et al. 2016).
EV_evidence_register.attribution: Watson et al. 2016 (cited in Ramsar BN10)

relationship.outcome_raw: wetland protection and restoration reduce wave damage and floods

context.note: Ramsar STRP key message (grey literature); protection and restoration stated together

EV_evidence_register.quote:
As extreme weather events such as storms, flooding, droughts and 
heat waves increase in frequency, wetland protection and restoration increases climate 
resilience by buffering communities from coastal storm surges, reducing wave damage 
and floods, and stabilizing shorelines, water supplies and local microclimates.
EV_evidence_register.attribution: Ramsar Convention STRP, Briefing Note 10 key message

relationship.unit: percent of solar energy transformed into sensible heat
relationship.outcome_raw: sensible-heat share over an intact wetland vs a drained wheat field (lower sensible heat = more local cooling); conservative ends of the stated ranges used

context.note: intact wetland vs drained field — the restoration target state vs the drained baseline, not a restored-site measurement

EV_evidence_register.quote:
Note the differences in solar energy 
transformation into sensible heat, 
reaching up to 60% to70% over a 
drained crop field compared to only 5% 
to10% over an intact wetland. In wetland 
landscapes, 70% to 80% of heat is 
dissipated via evapotranspiration. 
(Based on data measured in Trebon, 
Czech Republic. Source: Pokorný et al. 
2010b).
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: solar energy transformed into sensible heat
EV_evidence_register.attribution: Pokorný et al. 2010b (cited in Ramsar BN10, Figure 3)

relationship.outcome_raw: restored peatlands have lower carbon emission rates than degraded sites and over time can become net carbon sinks

context.note: emission-reduction magnitudes (Table 2, rewetting by prior land use) not encoded — no VONT id for GHG emission reduction

EV_evidence_register.quote:
Research has shown that, compared to degraded sites, restored peatlands have lower carbon 
emission rates and over time, can become net carbon sinks (Joosten et al. 2016).
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: net carbon sink after peatland restoration
EV_evidence_register.attribution: Joosten et al. 2016 (cited in Ramsar BN10)

relationship.outcome_raw: drained, cleared peat domes become vulnerable to long-burning wildfires

context.note: loss framing: drainage/conversion of peat raises fire vulnerability; supports rewetting as fire-risk reduction

EV_evidence_register.quote:
In the tropics, forested peat domes, where peat accumulates into thick, dome-shaped 
expanses, have been subject to clearing and agriculture, with many deforested for paper 
production, then drained and replanted with palm oil plantations. This liberates large 
quantities of carbon and makes them vulnerable to wildfires that, once started, can burn for 
years (Figure 3; Bell, 2016).
EV_evidence_register.attribution: Bell 2016 (news report, cited in Ramsar BN10)

relationship.outcome_raw: wetlands store precipitation and release it slowly, recharging groundwater

context.note: functional statement about wetlands generally (Ramsar key message), not a restoration measurement

EV_evidence_register.quote:
Wetlands store 
water from precipitation and slowly release it to the surrounding environment, which can 
also recharge groundwater aquifers and maintain atmospheric water cycles.
EV_evidence_register.attribution: Ramsar Convention STRP, Briefing Note 10 key message

relationship.unit: CTI (topographic wetness index scaled to an integer, see justification_quote)
relationship.direction: cells at or above the CTI threshold are treated as topographically suitable — they carry the potential to accumulate water and support wetlands; below it potential falls to the low class unless soils are poorly drained (combined with soil drainage in the potential-wetland-area index)

EV_evidence_register.quote:
By setting a threshold, we reduced both over and under 
prediction of locations where potential topographic conditions could support wetlands. 
Preliminary results from our comparison between CTI and the NWI data from Iowa and 
Georgia suggested that a CTI threshold of at least 550 would include all wetland types and 
much of the variation of CTI within each wetland type (Fig. 1).
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: Compound Topographic Index (CTI, = TWI scaled to integer) threshold for potential wetland area
EV_evidence_register.observed_dataset: CTI derived from USGS National Elevation Dataset (about 30 m)
EV_evidence_register.attribution: Horvath et al. 2017 — threshold calibrated against NWI wetlands in Iowa and Georgia
EV_evidence_register.justification_quote:
The CTI is calculated as [100 × ln (α/tan (β))] where 
100 is used to convert the value to an integer, α = ((flow accumulation +1) × pixel area 
(m2)), and β = slope (radians) (Beven and Kirkby, 1979).
EV_evidence_register.selection_justification:
In general, lower slope areas with sufficient overland runoff will collect water resulting in 
conditions with a greater potential to support wetlands.

relationship.direction: poorly and very poorly drained soils (longest, deepest saturation/inundation) indicate potential to support perennial wetlands; better-drained classes do not

EV_evidence_register.quote:
From the drainage classifications, poorly and very poorly drained soils are the 
most frequent, longest, and most deeply saturated or inundated of the soil drainage classes 
and thus should be considered an indicator of potential to support perennial types of 
wetlands.
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: SSURGO/STATSGO2 drainage class (poorly + very poorly drained, PVP)

relationship.unit: percent of soil map unit poorly or very poorly drained (PVP)
relationship.direction: at or above the PVP break point the soil represents the saturation and inundation duration needed for perennial wetlands; below it soils are more likely somewhat poorly drained and suit non-perennial wetland types, particularly in lower topographic positions — not an absolute exclusion

EV_evidence_register.quote:
Therefore, we selected cells 
having a PVP of 80% as a break point for further analyses. As a secondary evaluation, we 
compared our PVP soil drainage grid to a soil grid having ≥50% hydric conditions. The two 
were in agreement 85% of the time, suggesting that our greater than 80% PVP soil grid 
adequately represented both the saturation and inundation duration necessary to support 
perennial wetlands. Grid cells with less than 80% PVP soils would likely include somewhat 
poorly drained conditions, resulting in moderate saturation and inundation durations that 
would more successfully support non-perennial types of wetlands, particularly when located 
in lower topographic positions (Tiner, 1999).
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: percent poorly + very poorly drained soil per cell (PVP) break point
EV_evidence_register.attribution: Horvath et al. 2017; PVP grid cross-checked against hydric-soil grid

relationship.direction: joint soil-drainage × topographic-wetness classification of potential wetland area; poorly drained soil can compensate for low CTI (low class) and vice versa (moderate class)

EV_evidence_register.quote:
After defining the initial CTI threshold and the appropriate break points for PVP 
percentages, we combined the CTI and PVP layers into a single index layer of categorical 
classes of PWA: 1) high (CTI values ≥ 550 combined with 80–100% PVP of the summed 
soil components), 2) moderate (CTI values ≥ 550 combined with 1–79% PVP), 3) low (80–
100% PVP with CTI values ≤ 550), and 4) none (0% PVP or CTI values < 550 and < 80% 
PVP).
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: Potential Wetland Area (PWA) classes combining PVP soils and CTI
EV_evidence_register.attribution: Horvath et al. 2017 (EPA EnviroAtlas PWA layer)

relationship.direction: agricultural land (pasture/hay and cultivated crops) is the restorable target; developed land and large water bodies are excluded (impervious, commercially valuable, hydrology not restorable); natural covers are not targeted because they would not need extensive restoration — not because they are unsuitable

EV_evidence_register.quote:
To create the PRW-Ag layer, we combined the PWA classes with LULC classes from the 
2006 NLCD. LULC classes that were unlikely to be selected for wetland restoration, such as 
developed lands or large water bodies, were excluded from the selection. While wetland 
restoration can occur and provide benefits within other land use classes, such as open or low 
intensity development sites, these developed classes are also more likely to contain 
unsuitable land cover such as impervious surfaces and may also be more likely to be 
commercially valuable for other uses. In such cases, buffers may be a more suitable 
alternative to offset impacts to streams. It was assumed that natural land covers, such as 
forest, grassland, and existing wetlands, would not require extensive restoration. We, 
therefore, focused on agricultural land (pasture/hay [land cover code = 81] and cultivated 
crops [land cover code = 82]) in combination with the PWA classes.
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: NLCD 2006 land cover filter for potentially restorable wetlands on agricultural land (PRW-Ag)
EV_evidence_register.justification_quote:
Wetland restoration is more likely on certain landscapes (e.g., agriculture) than others 
due to the lack of substantive infrastructure and the potential for the restoration of hydrology;

relationship.direction: suitability declines with slope; above the maximum the cell is not suitable for wetland creation/restoration (authors note the cap is a local design choice — wetlands can occur on steeper slopes in New Zealand)

EV_evidence_register.quote:
Slope was the simplest derivative, since low slope angles are more suitable
for wetlands than steeper slopes. However, in New Zealand, wetlands can also occur on steeper
slopes. Therefore, in the current study, we deﬁned the maximum suitable slope for wetland as 3◦.
Smaller slopes were assigned a higher suitability for wetland development.
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: maximum suitable slope for wetland (LiDAR DEM, 1 m)
EV_evidence_register.attribution: Uuemaa et al. 2018 — GIS-MCA criterion (equal-weight linear sum of four criteria)
EV_evidence_register.justification_quote:
topography, since a wetland area needs to be generally ﬂat,
but natural landforms, such as swales and gullies, can facilitate wetland construction [8];

relationship.direction: monotonic increasing — higher TWI, higher wetland suitability; used only as one criterion because TWI alone was insufficient
relationship.scale: TWI deciles within the catchment rescaled 0 to 1 (catchment-relative, not a transferable threshold)

EV_evidence_register.quote:
Higher TWI values indicate higher soil moisture content and
also a higher suitability for wetland. TWI has been used effectively to predict soil moisture and has
also been tested for identifying wetlands by several authors [23,40]. However, TWI alone did not
provide sufﬁcient results. Therefore, we used TWI only as one parameter. TWI was calculated using
SAGA GIS [41]. Values of TWI were divided into deciles and assigned values from 0 to 1 to create
a suitability map.
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: topographic wetness index (SAGA GIS) decile suitability

relationship.direction: suitability decreases with distance from the (virtual) stream network and is zero beyond the maximum distance; closer to higher-order streams is better and the suitable band is wider along higher-order streams

EV_evidence_register.quote:
We created distance maps with a maximum distance of 125 m from the streams, and converted them
into suitability maps with each pixel having values from 0 to 1. The closer a site is to a higher-order
stream, the higher its suitability as a wetland site. In addition, the suitable area around higher-order
streams was wider than around the lower-order streams.
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: distance to streams (Strahler-order weighted) for in-stream wetlands
EV_evidence_register.observed_dataset: virtual stream network from LiDAR DEM flow accumulation
EV_evidence_register.attribution: Uuemaa et al. 2018 — in-stream wetland design only (off-stream options not considered)
EV_evidence_register.justification_quote:
Therefore, the potential wetland sites in our analysis occurred along the streams or drainage
ditches, and there is a higher probability for suitable wetland sites to exist along the higher-order
streams.

relationship.direction: a wetland with too small a contributing area is ineffective at reducing pollutant loads; sites below the minimum contributing area are not delineated

EV_evidence_register.quote:
The contributing area (i.e., the area that contributes water to the wetland) is an important criterion,
since wetlands with a too-small contributing area may be ineffective for decreasing pollutant
loads. (Here, we will focus on nitrogen pollution, but the same approach applies to most other
pollutants.) The minimum area we chose for this study was 50 ha.
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: minimum contributing (drainage) area for a created wetland
EV_evidence_register.attribution: Uuemaa et al. 2018 — effectiveness criterion for nutrient-interception wetlands

relationship.direction: suitability rises with distance from infrastructure (roads, farmsteads, other structures) and is full at the outer buffer — the wetland is created by flooding, so infrastructure must not be flooded (a physical-footprint constraint, not market access)

EV_evidence_register.quote:
We applied multiple 10-m buffers up to a distance of 100 m
from the infrastructure. The buffer values were converted into a suitability map in which distances
from the road were assigned values starting from 0 m (beside the road) and ending with 1 at a distance
of 100 m from the road.
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: distance to infrastructure (roads, farmsteads) to avoid flooding it
EV_evidence_register.observed_dataset: NZ topographic map roads + orthophoto-classified infrastructure
EV_evidence_register.justification_quote:
In the context of our study, we deﬁned constructing or restoring a wetland as ﬂooding the
suitable area. Flooding of infrastructure (e.g., roads, farmsteads) within that suitable area should be
avoided

EV_evidence_register.quote:
(vii) Major waterbodies: The waterbodies variable required only two classes (acceptable and not

EV_evidence_register.quote:
The soil and water conservation capacity of lands with a steep slope is limited [30]. Therefore, the
inﬂuence of topography on wetland rehabilitation should not be ignored [31]. The land slopes across
the entire SJP were generated from DEM data with a spatial resolution of 30 m provided by the United
States Geological Survey (USGS). We excluded the croplands having a slope greater than 5◦from the
wetland rehabilitation areas.

relationship.direction: cropland within the buffer of current open water (or in the smaller historic flood extent) is high rehabilitation priority; cropland outside it qualifies only if it lay in the larger later flood extent (medium)

Nonetheless,
these ﬂooded zones could reﬂect the suitable topographical and hydrological conditions for wetland
rehabilitation. Accordingly, ﬂooded areas in 1998 and 2013 were mapped by manual interpretation
from Landsat images. Since the ﬂooded area was smaller in 1998 than in 2013, we presumed the ﬂood
layer in 1998 and the waterbody in 2018 within a 300-m buﬀer zone were assigned a high rehabilitation
priority based on ﬁeld investigation and expert consultation, and the other ﬂooded area in 2013 was
given a medium rehabilitation priority.

relationship.outcome_raw: milk production in the El Nino year with la menor precipitación en varias décadas rose relative to the previous year after conversion to intensive silvopasture, without irrigation

context.severity_cue: la menor precipitación en varias décadas

EV_evidence_register.quote: Para el caso de la Reserva Natural El Hatico, el cambio hacia SSPi permitió eliminar el riego en los potreros sin efectos notables sobre la producción. Esto se logró incluso durante al menos dos eventos de El Niño, caracterizados por una fuerte reducción de la precipitación en Colombia, incluyendo el año 2009, en el que se registró la menor precipitación en varias décadas (440 mm anuales), a pesar de lo cual se logró un aumento del 10% en la producción de leche con respecto al año anterior (Murgueitio et al. 2011). (English: At El Hatico Nature Reserve, the switch to intensive silvopastoral systems made it possible to eliminate pasture irrigation with no notable effect on production. This was achieved even during at least two El Niño events, characterised by a strong reduction of rainfall in Colombia, including 2009, which recorded the lowest rainfall in several decades (440 mm per year), despite which milk production increased by 10% relative to the previous year (Murgueitio et al. 2011).)
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: producción de leche en año El Niño

relationship.outcome_raw: field soil moisture and water retention higher under intensive silvopasture than under treeless pasture

Las características en- contradas en las pasturas sin árboles están asociadas a una reducción de la aireación del suelo, de su capacidad para almacenar agua y de su nivel de infiltración, lo cual tiene efectos notables sobre el ciclo hidrológico local (Camargo et al. 2010). (English: Likewise, intensive silvopastoral systems contributed to soil water retention, since field moisture was higher in soils under these systems than in pastures without trees. EV_evidence_register.quote: Betancourt et ál. (2003) mencionan que la producción de leche de animales bajo sistemas con alta densidad de árboles se incrementó en 29% en comparación con animales que pastoreaban potreros con baja cobertura arbórea, los autores lo atribuyen a la reducción en el es- trés calórico y a la mayor cantidad de follaje y frutos en los primeros potreros, en otros trabajos se encontraron incrementos superiores a 15% en producción de leche en animales que se pastoreaban en sistemas silvopasto- riles, comparado con animales que estuvieron a pleno sol (Souza et ál., 2000). (2003) report that milk production of animals in systems with high tree density increased by 29% compared with animals grazing pastures with low tree cover; the authors attribute it to reduced heat stress and greater foliage and fruit in the former pastures; other studies found increases above 15% in milk production of animals grazing silvopastoral systems compared with animals in full sun (Souza et al., 2000).)

relationship.outcome_raw: dry-season liveweight gain of cattle on high tree-density pasture vs low-cover pasture

context.note: narrative review in Revista de Medicina Veterinaria (Universidad de La Salle)

EV_evidence_register.quote: Los periodos de sequía en el trópico se caracterizan por altas temperaturas y forrajes de baja calidad que son poco aprovechados por los animales, los cua- les en algunos casos pierden peso en estas épocas. Restrepo (2001) encontró en la época seca mayores ganancias de peso (2 a 5%) en animales que pasto- reaban potreros con alta densidad de árboles, que aquellos que estaban en zonas de baja cobertura, esto se puede atribuir, en parte, a mayores tiempos de pastoreo y rumia producto de la reducción del es- trés calórico. (English: Drought periods in the tropics are characterised by high temperatures and low-quality forage that animals use poorly, and in some cases they lose weight in these periods. Restrepo (2001) found higher weight gains (2 to 5%) in the dry season in animals grazing pastures with high tree density than in those in low-cover areas, which can be attributed in part to longer grazing and rumination times resulting from reduced heat stress.)
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: ganancia de peso en época seca

relationship.outcome_raw: midday air temperature under tree groups, single trees and live fences vs open pasture (tree groups largest reduction, live fences smallest)

context.note: narrative review in Revista de Medicina Veterinaria (Universidad de La Salle)

EV_evidence_register.quote: Navas (2003) encontró diferencias de temperatura, bajo la copas de árboles de diferentes arreglos silvo- pastoriles (árboles en grupo, árboles individuales y cercas vivas) y áreas de potrero abierto en las horas del día de mayor temperatura ambiental (tabla 2), se observan diferencias de 3,6 ° C, 2,9 ° C y 1,7 ° C menos respectivamente con relación a las áreas de potrero abierto. Sistemas de árboles en grupo o bos- quetes tienen un efecto mayor sobre la reducción de la temperatura. (English: Navas (2003) found temperature differences under the crowns of trees in different silvopastoral arrangements (tree groups, individual trees and live fences) and open pasture during the hottest hours of the day (Table 2): 3.6 °C, 2.9 °C and 1.7 °C lower respectively than open pasture. Tree groups or copses have a greater effect on temperature reduction.)
